record.original_question: Let M_n be the n-th term of the mirror sequence formed by writing the descending string from n to 1 immediately followed by the ascending string from 2 back to n, so the sequence begins 1, 212, 32123, 4321234, 543212345, and continues in the same way. Are there infinitely many prime numbers among these mirror-sequence terms, or only finitely many?

evidence.quote: Question: How many of them are primes?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For each positive integer $n$, define $M_n$ to be the integer whose decimal representation is obtained by concatenating, in order, the digit strings of the integers $n, n-1, n-2, \dots, 2, 1, 2, 3, \dots, n-1, n$. Thus $M_1 = 1$, $M_2 = 212$, $M_3 = 32123$, $M_4 = 4321234$, $M_5 = 543212345$, and in general $M_n$ is the "descend-then-ascend" concatenation $n(n-1)\cdots 21 2\cdots(n-1)n$ (where for $n \geq 10$ each integer contributes all of its decimal digits to the concatenation).

Determine whether the set $\{n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : M_n \text{ is prime}\}$ is infinite or finite.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears to be open. The closely related Smarandache concatenation sequence 1, 121, 12321, ... (OEIS A173426) has been computationally examined: only two probable primes are known (the 20-digit term and a 17350-digit probable prime), with no further primes found for n up to 60000, and only heuristic arguments (attributed to D. Broadhurst) suggest infinitely many primes. No proof of either finiteness or infinitude is known for the analogous "descend then ascend" mirror variant. No rigorous resolution of the primality question for the mirror sequence was located.

status_evidence.title: A173426 - OEIS
status_evidence.snippet: The first prime is the 20-digit a(10) = 12345678910987654321. A 17350-digit probable prime is the 2446th term. No others for n<60000. Broadhurst gives heuristic arguments suggesting infinitely many primes.
status_evidence.claim: Primality in the closely related Smarandache concatenation mirror sequence is unresolved; only heuristics suggest infinitely many primes.

status_evidence.title: FLORENTIN SMARANDACHE SEQUENCES OF NUMBERS INVOLVED IN UNSOLVED PROBLEMS
status_evidence.snippet: Mirror sequence 1, 212, 32123, 4321234, ... Question: How many of them are primes?
status_evidence.claim: The primality question for the mirror sequence is posed as an open problem.
